about: What the Kotlin backend's `LuaScriptEngine` answers differently from
ECMA-262, case by case, against the shared table beside this file.
The engine that list is about is Lua 5.4 with `sce-build`'s ECMAScript
frontend PARSING the author's ECMAScript and lowering it, reached
through `sce_lua_jni` — the same staticlib the C++ engine links, built
by the same `cmake/SCEBuildLowering.cmake`, so two backends cannot
lower against two frontends. `EngineFactory` offers it beside Rhino and
QuickJS as an equal option, so a consumer may pick it.
It reached that frontend through `EcmaScriptToLuaTransformer`, which
rewrote the same text without parsing it, and every entry this list ever
held was that difference. A pass that replaces text cannot say where an
operand ends: `a && b` could not yield its left operand, `-7 % 3` could
not truncate, `5 ^ 3` came back 125. The list is now EMPTY because the
frontend answers all of them — not because the rewriter was repaired.
⚠ EMPTY IS NOT RETIRED. The rewriter is still compiled in and is still
the FALLBACK behind every lowering entry point, so text the frontend
refuses is rewritten rather than refused. That is the state the C++
engine passed through before its own `retire-rewriter` row closed, and
the two claims are separate on purpose: what an empty list says is that
the frontend answers the 98 cases of the shared table, and what
retirement would say is that there is no second answer left. The seam
document's `kotlin-retire-rewriter` row is where the second claim will
be held; until it closes, an expression outside the shared table that
the frontend refuses still gets the rewriter's guess.
Empty is a legal state rather than a broken read, and the suites that
hold it may not require it to be non-empty — that is the finish line.
What still has to be true is that something OPENS it, which
`ecma262_scoreboard_contract` asserts by sweeping every tracked file for
a reader.
This file exists because the count used to live in prose.
`EcmaScriptSemanticsTest` used to assert only that the failure set was
NOT EMPTY — satisfied by one disagreement and by fifty — while
`LuaScriptEngine`'s KDoc carried "27 of its 58" under a sentence
claiming that test held the number. It held none, and the shared table
had grown to 98 cases. The real number was 46 on 2026-08-29, 44 by the
end of that day, and 0 on 2026-08-30. A list the test reads cannot drift
that way. An entry here that starts agreeing fails as loudly as a case
that starts disagreeing, so neither direction passes unnoticed.
Separate from the C++ list on purpose, and neither may be derived from
the other: the two engines are two Luas reached by two runtimes, and
that they now share a frontend is a measurement rather than a
definition. They were not the same size while each had its own rewriter
— 23 against 44 — and that difference is itself a thing no prose count
could have shown.
No `needs` field, unlike the C++ list. There it says what closing an
entry would take, and each value was an analysis of that rewriter.
Nobody did that analysis for this one, and with the list empty a guessed
value would be an unmeasured claim about entries that no longer exist.
`diverges_on` says WHICH PATH into the engine an entry is about, the same
way `lua_engine_divergences.json` says it, and `paths` below is the set an
entry may name:
runtime-rewriter     The artifact hands the engine the AUTHOR'S
ECMAScript and the engine lowers it on the spot.
The name is the rewriter's because that is what
used to do the lowering; what does it now is the
frontend, reached at run time. Held
two-directionally by `EcmaScriptSemanticsTest`.
build-time-lowering  `sce-build`'s ECMAScript frontend emitted Lua and
the artifact hands the engine that, so nothing is
lowered at run time. Held two-directionally by
`LoweredEcma262Test`, which asks the WHOLE shared
table rather than this list — a path's divergences
cannot be enumerated by a list built from the
other path's.
So an entry stays while ANY path still answers it differently, and it
LEAVES when `diverges_on` would be empty.
`paths` is not decoration: a value naming a path nothing measures would
be a claim no lane can fault. `ecma262_scoreboard_contract` compares it
against what `sce-build` derives for this backend, so the day Kotlin
gains or loses a path this key and the entries under it are held to the
change instead of outliving it.
The count is deliberately written nowhere in this file. It lives in the
table under `<!-- sce:kotlin-lowering-dividend -->` in
`docs/SCE_LUA_TRANSLATION_SEAM.md`, which is the copy a person reads,
and that same lane re-derives it from this list on every push.
